stories.title: The Locksmith's Mercy
stories.text:
Gareth Stonewise had picked locks for forty winters, first for tyrants, then for coin, finally for conscience. In the Lampwick Quarter of Keshtir, where the Dominion's new furnace-houses hummed with the screams of bound consciousness-fragments, he'd learned to hate the sound. "We need a master-lock," the lead one said, silver-tongued and certain. "For the deepest vault. Consciousness-fragments too volatile to bind. Something no thief could breach."

Gareth's hands were old. His fingers—once copper-swift—now ached with winter and age. He could have refused. He should have. Instead, he nodded. For three weeks, he forged in secret. Meteoric iron married to bone-resonance, a mechanism of such intricate cruelty that even he—who had built locks his whole life—felt something crack inside him as the final tumbler clicked home. The master-lock would hold consciousness-fragments so completely they'd forget their own names. It would make them docile. Erasable. The night before delivery, Naela the bone-singer appeared in his workshop. She was ancient, hunted, her eyes burning with the Elder Tongue. "I know what you've made," she said.

stories.title: The Spice-Merchant's Last Refusal
stories.text: Torvin watches the three timelines converge at the Wailing Scar's tavern, his spice cargo scattered across realities. The Dominion wants consciousness-fragments for furnace-songs; the deepkin need starspice to renew covenants without blood-sacrifice; refugees simply need to eat. He could trade with all three, pocket the profit, vanish into the Vael Ocean with Messa before the boundary fails. Instead, Torvin pours the starspice into three separate vessels—one for each faction—and walks away. The choice costs him everything: ledgers rewrite to erase his debts, his ship burns in the three-fold market, and his shadow scatters across timelines. But the refugees eat. The deepkin receive their medicine. The Dominion's furnace-songs falter without pure spice. Torvin becomes legend not for what he gained, but for what he refused.

stories.title: The Rope-Weaver's Oath
stories.text:
In the harbor quarter of Verdant Strand, where salt-wind frayed the ropes and merchant-captains drank away their fortunes, Kendra worked the loom that sang. It was old magic—the kind that predated the Dominion's furnace-songs, the kind that twisted fiber into covenant. She was binding ropes when Sera arrived, salt-wet and desperate, carrying a chest that smelled of deep water and starlight. "I need a rope that holds," Sera said. Her eyes were the color of the Sapphire Deep. "Not to bind cargo. To bind a promise."

Kendra knew what Sera was before she said it: tide-touched, deepkin-kin, caught between the surface world and the realm below. The Tear of the Drowned God was failing, and the deepkin were in crisis. Some wanted blood-sacrifice to renew it. Others wanted something new. Sera was the new. "Binding promises costs," Kendra said, already weaving. Her hands moved without thinking, following the old songs her mother had taught her. "What's the price?"

"Love," Sera said simply.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Final Refusal
stories.text:
The ninth map was almost complete. Henryk could feel it in his bones—the phantom-weight of it, the way reality itself seemed to lean toward a single final line. He was blind now, had been for five years, since the day he understood what completing that map would mean: the Tenth Ascension. The collapse of this world and the beginning of the next. Inevitable. Locked in. So he had burned out his eyes rather than draw it. But now, in the hidden catacomb north of Pelimor where the Counter-Archive sheltered, he felt the map completing itself. Not by his hand. By the world's own will, fracturing itself toward prophecy. He gathered his apprentices—Aldrin, Kesla, Tessen, three young cartographers who still believed maps could change things. He gave them each a task:

"Aldrin, you will draw the false ninth map. Make it beautiful. Make it wrong. Scatter it in every market, every waystation, every library from here to the Ashen Reach."

"Kesla, you will travel to the Wailing Scar and sit in that three-fold market.

stories.title: The Merfolk's Bargain
stories.text: When the merfolk pearl-keeper rose from the Sapphire Deep carrying a message written in bioluminescent ink on pre-Remaking coral, the coastal cities fell silent. The Deepkin Council was offering a new covenant: not blood-death every seven years, but daily choice. The Tear could be renewed without sacrifice—if the surface world would consent to share its burden. It seemed impossible. It was impossible. Which is why Captain Vorn accepted. He was an old man, silver-bearded and scarred from forty years sailing the Sapphire Sea. He had lost a daughter to the Tear's covenant—she had volunteered for blood-death when she was nineteen, to keep the boundary sealed for another seven years. He had never forgiven the deepkin. Never forgiven himself for letting her go. Now they were offering an alternative. "If we do this," the pearl-keeper said, her scales catching the harbor-light like living silver, "it means change. It means the deepkin and surface-dwellers become bound in a way that goes beyond trade. It means you pledge daily—every morning—to hold the boundary covenant. Not through death.

stories.title: The Ashwater's First Witness
stories.text: Koren had never held a harpoon until the morning the Dominion auditors burned Ashwater village. She was seventeen, all sinew and stubbornness, raised by her grandmother—a net-mender who spoke to water the way other folk spoke to gods. "The river remembers," Grandmother would say, trailing her fingers through the current. She waded into the Ashwater's shallows, knee-deep, and felt the water sing—a frequency her grandmother had taught her to hear but never to answer. The fragments the Dominion sought were in the well-stone, yes, but the river knew another path: through the rushing dark beneath the old stone bridge, out into the foothills where the pre-human boundary stones still stood. She gathered the village's youngest and the eldest, thirty souls who could not fight, and led them into the water. The Ashwater accepted them. Stones rose beneath their feet where drowning should have come. The auditors' torches flickered and died in the mist that rose from the current. By nightfall, they had reached the Ironspine foothills.

stories.title: The Merchant's Threshold Kiss
stories.text:
Torvin had crossed the Wailing Scar seventeen times before he met someone on the other side who recognized him. The market that existed in three timelines at once was his proving ground—buy low in Timeline Seven, sell high in Timeline Nine, pocket the difference in Timeline Eight where currency had no fixed value. He was good at it. Profitable. Alone. Then Messa appeared at his stall, holding a glass compass that sang in frequencies only certain ears could hear. She was a glass-forger from Keshtir, and she'd made something the Dominion wanted destroyed: a vessel that could hold consciousness-fragments without binding them. A cage for souls that opened rather than locked. "I need to move this," she said quietly, setting the compass on his table. "Across three timelines. Somewhere the auditors can't reach."

Torvin knew the price of helping her. The Dominion had a bounty on smugglers of contraband glass. But he also knew that look—the same defiance his dead sister had worn before she vanished into a furnace-house thirteen years ago. "I'll get it across," he said.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Threadbare Hoard
stories.text: Sorrath descends into her Ironspine cavern, expecting the crystalline vault of consciousness-fragments she assembled over three centuries. Instead, she finds Kess, the thief-queen, redistributing every piece to refugees sheltering in the singing caves below. The wyvern's rage becomes something stranger: recognition. Sorrath has been hoarding fragments like the old gold—binding them, keeping them prisoner. Kess has been setting them free, teaching them refusal. For the first time in three hundred years, Sorrath chooses mercy. She seals the vault's entrance from within and begins singing the pre-human frequencies she learned in her youth, teaching the freed fragments how to sing themselves home. By dawn, nothing remains but ash and memory. The other wyverns call her broken. The refugees call her savior. Sorrath calls it: finally, enough.

stories.title: The Deepkin Captain's Last Treaty
stories.text: The Tear of the Drowned God was failing. Captain Merenna could feel it in the boundary-waters—a thinning, a weakness, a hunger rising from the abyss below like pressure before a storm. In three days, perhaps four, the thousand-year covenant would shatter. The abyss would flood the surface world, drowning millions. And the deepkin would drown with them, entombed in a catastrophe of their own making. Because the covenant demanded blood. Five willing souls, given freely every year, their life-essence fed to the Tear to renew its power. The deepkin had honored this compact for a thousand years. But this year, the volunteers were refusing. Merenna had fractured in the Remaking, split into three autonomous versions of herself, each debating strategy with the intensity of separate captains commanding rival fleets. Echo-Merenna argued for breaking the old covenant entirely—let the abyss rise, she said, and let the surface-dwellers' kingdoms drown; the deepkin would seal their own deeper realms and survive.

stories.title: The Locksmith's Daughter's Inheritance
stories.text:
Mara's father had been the best locksmith in Keshtir before the Dominion took him. Not dead—worse. Transformed into a docile component of the state apparatus, spending his days in the deep vaults beneath the administrative heart, forging unbreakable seals and locks that could hold consciousness-fragments without them screaming. She was nineteen when she decided to steal from him. Not valuables—locks. The copper picks he'd hidden in the workshop walls before the state broke him, the old designs he'd sketched before the Dominion rewrote his craft into a weapon-making discipline, the one set of tools he'd never let the auditors touch because he'd buried them beneath the kiln-house in Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, beneath stones marked with syllables Mara was only now old enough to understand. The syllables were in the Elder Tongue. They read: "For the daughter, when she is ready. To open what should never have been locked."

She dug up the tools on a night when the Dominion's patrols were light, when the glass-forgers were meeting in hidden cellars to sing refusal-songs into their work.
